questions.q: If the domain of the function $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\cos^{- 1}\sqrt{{x}^{2} - x + 1}}{\sqrt{\sin^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{2x - 1}{2}\right)}}$ is the interval $( \alpha, \beta ] ,$ then $\alpha + \beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Given function is $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\cos^{- 1}\sqrt{{x}^{2} - x + 1}}{\sqrt{\sin^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{2x - 1}{2}\right)}}$

For, $\sin^{- 1}x \text{ and } \cos^{1}x$ to be defined $- 1 \le x \le 1$ and for $\sqrt{f\left(x\right)}$ to be defined $f\left(x\right) \ge 0$ and the denominator of any expression can never be zero.

Thus, to define the domain of the given function, we have

$- 1 \le \sqrt{{x}^{2} - x + 1} \le 1, {x}^{2} - x + 1 \ge 0$ and $\sin^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{2x - 1}{2}\right) > 0$

Taking the common values and using the range of $\sin^{- 1}x$ i.e. for positive values $0 < \sin^{- 1}x \le \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ we get

$0 \le {x}^{2} - x + 1 \le 1$ and $0 < \sin^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{2x - 1}{2}\right) \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

$⇒ {x}^{2} - x \le 0$ and $0 < \dfrac{2x - 1}{2} \le 1$

$⇒ x\left(x - 1\right) \le 0$ and $0 < 2x - 1 \le 2$

$⇒ x \in [ 0, 1 ]$ and $1 < 2x \le 3$

$⇒ x \in \left[0, 1\right]$ and $\dfrac{1}{2} < x \le \dfrac{3}{2}$

Now, taking intersection, we get $x \in \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 1\right]$

Given, domain of the function is $\left(\alpha, \beta\right] = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 1\right]$

$⇒ \alpha = \dfrac{1}{2}, \beta = 1$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta = \dfrac{3}{2} .$

questions.q: Let $A = { 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 } .$ Then the number of bijective functions $f: A \to A$ such that $f ( 1 ) + f ( 2 ) = 3 - f ( 3 )$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given the set $A = { 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 } .$

And, also a function $f: A \to A$ satisfying $f ( 1 ) + f ( 2 ) = 3 - f ( 3 )$

$⇒ f ( 1 ) + f ( 2 ) + f ( 3 ) = 3$

Since, the range of the function is also $A,$ hence the only possibility satisfying the given condition is: $0 + 1 + 2 = 3$

We know that, the number of arrangements of $n$ objects at $n$ places is $n ! .$

Since, the given function is bijective i.e. one-one and onto, hence, the elements $1, 2, 3$ in the domain can be mapped with only $0, 1, 2$ in the co-domain in $3 !$ ways and the remaining $5$ elements $0, 4, 5, 6, 7$ in the domain can be mapped with any of the remaining $5$ elements $3, 4, 5, 6, 7$ in $5 !$ ways.

So, the number of bijective functions are $= 3 ! \times 5 ! = 6 \times 120 = 720 .$

questions.solution:
$f ( x ) + g ( x ) = \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{1 - x},$ domain $\left[0, 1\right]$

$f ( x ) - g ( x ) = \sqrt{x} - \sqrt{1 - x},$ domain $\left[0, 1\right]$

$g ( x ) - f ( x ) = \sqrt{1 - x} - \sqrt{x},$ domain $\left[0, 1\right]$

$\dfrac{g ( x )}{f ( x )} = \dfrac{\sqrt{1 - x}}{\sqrt{x}},$ domain $( 0, 1 ]$

So, common domain is $\left(0, 1\right)$

questions.q: Let $f, g: N \to N$ such that $f\left(n + 1\right) = f\left(n\right) + f\left(1\right) ∀ n \in N$ and $g$ be any arbitrary function. Which of the following statements is NOT true?
options: If $f$ is onto, then $f\left(n\right) = n ∀ n \in N$
If $g$ is onto, then $fog$ is one-one
If $fog$ is one-one, then $g$ is one-one
questions.solution:

General term = ${T}_{n} = f ( 1 ) + ( n - 1 ) f ( 1 ) = nf ( 1 )$

$⇒ f\left(n\right) = nf\left(1\right)$⇒ f$ is one-one

Now, Let $f\left(g\left({x}_{2}\right)\right) = f\left(g\left({x}_{1}\right)\right)$

$⇒ g\left({x}_{2}\right) = g\left({x}_{1}\right)$ (as $f$ is one-one)

$⇒ {x}_{1} = {x}_{2}$ (as $fog$ is one-one)

$⇒ g$ is one-one

For $f$ to be onto, $f ( n )$ should take all the values of natural numbers.

As $f ( x )$ is increasing, $f ( 1 ) = 1$

$⇒ f ( n ) = n$

Now, $f\left(g\left(n\right)\right) = g\left(n\right)f\left(1\right)$

may be many-one if

$g\left(n\right)$ is many-one

So “if $g$ is onto, then $fog$ is one-one” is incorrect.

questions.q: Suppose a differentiable function $f\left(x\right)$ satisfies the identity $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + x{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}y,$ for all real $x$ and $y$. If $\lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{x} = 1,$ then ${f}^{'}\left(3\right)$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$∵ \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{x} = 1 ⇒ f ' \left(0\right) = 1$

$f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + x{y}^{2} + {x}^{2}y$

Differentiate w.r.t. $x$ keeping $y$ constant

$f ' \left(x + y\right) = f ' \left(x\right) + 0 + {y}^{2} + 2xy$

put $y = - x$

$f ' \left(0\right) = f ' \left(x\right) + {x}^{2} - 2{x}^{2}$

$1 = f ' \left(x\right) - {x}^{2}$

$f ' \left(x\right) = 1 + {x}^{2}$

$f ' \left(3\right) = 10$.

$= 4$ when $x = 5n + 4, n \in N$

questions.q: Let $a, b, c \in R$ . If $f\left(x\right) = a{x}^{2} + bx + c$ is such that $a + b + c = 3$ and $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + xy, ∀ x, y \in R$ , then $\mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10} f ( n )$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Given, $f\left(x + y\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(y\right) + xy ∀ x, y \in R$

Put $y = 1$, we get

$⇒ f\left(x + 1\right) = f\left(x\right) + f\left(1\right) + x$

$⇒ f\left(x + 1\right) - f\left(x\right) = 3 + x$

On taking Sigma on both sides

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{x = 1}^{n - 1}\left(f\left(x + 1\right) - f\left(x\right)\right) = \mathop{∑}_{x = 1}^{n - 1}\left(3 + x\right)$

$⇒ \left(f\left(2\right) - f\left(1\right)\right) + \left(f\left(3\right) - f\left(2\right)\right) + \left(f\left(4\right) - f\left(3\right)\right) + \left(f\left(5\right) - f\left(4\right)\right) + . . . . . . + \left(f\left(n\right) - f\left(n - 1\right)\right)$

$= 3\left(n - 1\right) + \dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)n}{2}$

$⇒ f\left(n\right) - f\left(1\right) = 3\left(n - 1\right) + \dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)n}{2}$

$⇒ f\left(n\right) - 3 = 3\left(n - 1\right) + \dfrac{\left(n - 1\right)n}{2}$

$⇒ f\left(n\right) = \dfrac{{n}^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{5n}{2}$

Again taking Sigma on both the sides

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}f\left(n\right) = \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}\left(\dfrac{{n}^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{5n}{2}\right)$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}f\left(n\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} . \dfrac{10 . 11 . 21}{6} + \dfrac{5}{2} . \dfrac{10 . 11}{2}$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{n = 1}^{10}f\left(n\right) = 330$.

questions.q: The function $f\left(x\right) = \left|sin 4x\right| + \left|cos 2x\right|,$ is a periodic function with a fundamental period
questions.solution:
Given $f\left(x\right) = \left|sin4x\right| + \left|cos2x\right|$

We know that the period of $\left|sin x\right|$ is $\pi$ and also if $f\left(x\right)$ is a periodic function with fundamental period $T,$ then the fundamental period of $f\left(kx\right)$ is $\dfrac{T}{\left|k\right|} .$

$⇒ {T}_{1} =$period of $\left|\text{sin4}\text{x}\right| = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Also, we know that the period of $\left|cosx\right|$ is $\pi$

$⇒ {T}_{2} =$Period of $\left|cos2x\right| = \dfrac{\pi}{2}$

Again, we know that the period of the sum or difference of two periodic functions is the $L . C . M .$ of their periods.

So, the period of $f ( x )$ is $L . C . M .$ of the periods of $\left|sin4x\right|$ and $\left|cos2x\right|$ i.e. the $L . C . M . \left({T}_{1}, {T}_{2}\right)$

Now, $L . C . M . \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = \dfrac{L . C . M . \left(\pi, \pi\right)}{H . C . F . \left(4, 2\right)} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} .$

questions.q: The range of the function $f(x)=\frac{x}{1+|x|}, x \in R$, is
questions.solution:
$f(x)=\frac{x}{1+|x|}, x \in R$
If $x>0,|x|=x \Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{x}{1+x}$ which is not defined for $x=-1$
If $x < 0,|x|=-x \Rightarrow f(x)=\frac{x}{1-x}$ which is not defined for $x=1$ Thus $f(x)$ defined for all values of $\mathrm{R}$ except 1 and $-1$
Hence, range $=(-1,1)$.

questions.solution:
Given $f(x)=x^3+5 x+1$
Now $f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^2+5>0, \forall x \in R$\therefore \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ is strictly increasing function

$\operatorname{Lt}_{x \rightarrow-\infty} f(x)=-\infty$ and $\operatorname{Lt}_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x)=\infty$\therefore \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})$ takes every value between $-\infty$ and $\infty$.
Thus, $f(x)$ is onto function.
